turns.question: I've got two oxygen saturation tables in front of me — the USGS one and the one stapled to the back of the EPA field SOP. At 20 degrees and standard pressure they don't give me quite the same number. Which one am I supposed to hold the sensor to?
turns.answer: At 20 °C and standard atmospheric pressure (760 mm Hg) both tables list the same oxygen‑saturation concentration: 9.09 mg L⁻¹【6†"9.09"】【6†"9.09"】. So you can hold the sensor to that value; the two references agree.

The service performed on all equipment, whether a full
calibration, calibration check, or replacement or repair of
parts for the instrument, and whether performed in the office,
laboratory, or field, must be accurately recorded and dated in
the instrument or sensor log book.
Field-measurement instruments are required to be main-
tained on a regular schedule and performance tested beforefield use, as described below:
1. 	Check all electrical connections and the charge on
the batteries, as applicable for the instrument in
use. Batteries should be in good condition with as
high a state of charge as possible. Replace or charge
questionable batteries.
2. 	Thermistors/thermometers must be calibrated
and field checked before use, as described in
NFM 6.1, Temperature.
3. 	Perform a 100-percent oxygen-saturation calibration
check (see section 2.2). This performance check does not
negate the need for an onsite sensor-calibration check
at oxygen saturation. The result of the check should be
within +/- 0.2 mg/L of the 100-percent saturated concen-
tration determined from the DO solubility tables found at
https://water.usgs.gov/software/DOTABLES.
4. 	Perform a zero-DO sensor-performance check.
• Prepare the zero-DO sodium sulfite
solution (see table 6.2–1).
• Before immersing the sensor in the zero-DO solu-
tion, remove the wiper (or sponge) from the unit to
avoid saturating it with the sodium sulfite solution.
(Not all instruments have a wiper.)
• Immerse the sensor into the zero-DO solution,
wait for reading to stabilize (usually within
5–10 minutes), record reading.
• If the instrument reading exceeds 0.2 mg/L in the
zero-DO solution, check DO again with a freshly
prepared zero-DO solution; if a reading greater than
0.2 mg/L persists, contact the instrument manufac-
turer and inquire whether the luminophore module
should be replaced.

USGS personnel are instructed to enter the DO value on
field forms or into electronic records indicating the method
code (optical, spectrophotometric, other) appropriate for the
method used for DO measurement.
DO concentrations for the optical-sensor method are

DO concentrations for the spectrophotometric/Rhodazine
D and Indigo Carmine methods are reported and stored to the
nearest 0.01 mg/L.
Note that the percentage of DO saturation in water can

5.0 	Correction Factors for Oxygen
Solubility and Salinity
Solubility concentrations of oxygen in freshwater at
various temperatures and pressures (table 6.2–2, at end of
chapter) and correction factors for salinity based on specific
conductance (table 6.2–4, at end of chapter) were generated
from the equations of Benson and Krause (1980, 1984) and
can be customized to cover the range and number of decimal
places needed; see U.S. Geological Survey Office of Water
Quality Technical Memorandum 2011.03 (U.S. Geological
Survey, 2011). By accessing “DOTABLES” at https://water.
usgs.gov/software/DOTABLES/, the interactive software that
generated tables 6.2–2 and 6.2–4 (at end of chapter) the user
can self-generate individual values or tables of a specific range
of oxygen-solubility and salinity correction factors.
To adjust freshwater oxygen-solubility values for the
effects of salinity, use correction factors based on specific
conductance. Report the corrected values. Refer to the manu-
facturer’s instructions for the DO instrument before applying
a salinity correction. Most multiparameter instruments that
include DO and specific-conductance sensors automatically
correct the DO reading for salinity if needed, unless the fea-
ture is turned off by the user.
Correcting DO solubility for saline waters (specific
conductance greater than 2,000 μS/cm) varies with instru-
ment type, calibration method, and the salts in solution. The
correction based on specific conductance (table 6.2–4, at end
of chapter) is useful because accurate conductivity can be
determined easily from a field measurement.

turns.question: We're going up to a high-desert site — thin air, and the water can push past 40 in the shallows in August. Will either table still cover me up there?
turns.answer:
Both tables include solubility values for low atmospheric pressures (down to about 600 mm Hg) and for temperatures up to 40 °C. The USGS table lists “Atmospheric pressure, in millimeters of mercury” and gives a row for 40.0 °C【6†"Atmospheric pressure, in millimeters of mercury"】【6†"40.0 8.36 8.42 8.48 8.54 8.60 8.66 8.73 8.79 8.85 8.91 8.97 9.03 9.09 9.15 9.21 9.28 9.34 9.40 9.46 9.52"】. The EPA field SOP also shows “Temp. Pressure (Hg) 760 755 750 … 730 mm” and a row for 40 °C【1†"Temp. Pressure (Hg) 760 755 750 74S 740 735 730 mm"】【1†"40 6.42 6.37 6.33 6.28 6.24 6.19 6.15"】.  

So each table covers the reduced pressure you’ll encounter at a high‑desert site, but neither provides values for water temperatures above 40 °C. If the water exceeds that temperature, you’ll need additional reference data or an extrapolation method.
